title: The call
hookLine: the leader calls the congregation to bless, and they answer; it needs a minyan

lines: MUCH OF THE SERVICE WORKS ALONE.
cards: Much of the morning service can be prayed alone at a kitchen table. The blessings for waking, the study, the psalms: they work with a congregation of one. A few moments don't.
The Kaddish is one. And right after the half Kaddish that follows Yishtabach comes another. The prayer leader turns toward the room and calls out two words, and the room has to answer.
With fewer than ten people there, the call isn't said at all. It's the hinge of the morning: before it, the verses of song; after it, the Shema and its blessings.

teach.b: The leader says: Barchu et Adonai hamevorach. Bless the LORD, the blessed one.

teach.h: THE ROOM ANSWERS, THE LEADER TOO.
teach.b: The congregation answers: Baruch Adonai hamevorach le'olam va'ed. Blessed is the LORD, the blessed one, forever and ever. Then the leader repeats the answer, so the one who called isn't left out of the response.
Many people bow as they say it. It's the same call that opens a reading from the Torah. The idea of calling others to praise is old.

teach.h: O MAGNIFY THE LORD WITH ME.
teach.b: A psalm says, in the old Jewish translation: "O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt His name together." With me. Together.

teach.h: TEN FOR A MATTER OF HOLINESS.
teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, teaches that any matter of holiness needs at least ten people, a minyan.
It learns the number by a chain of verses: the word congregation, used for the ten spies in the wilderness, links to the verse that says God will be hallowed among the children of Israel.

So a congregation, for these purposes, starts at ten. Communities differ on who counts toward the ten: in Orthodox practice, ten adult men; in other communities, ten adults of any gender. All of them share the shape.
Many answer. And the caller answers too, so nobody in the room is left out of the blessing.

how: In a minyan, the prayer leader calls out Barchu before the Shema and its blessings in the morning and evening services, and before each Torah reading; the congregation answers aloud, and many bow.

o: the leader's call to bless, answered by all
the blessing said over bread before a meal
a blessing said alone before going to sleep

p: ten, for a matter of holiness

s: Barchu can be said by one person praying alone
it's a call and an answer; it needs a minyan of ten.
the leader repeats the congregation's answer
so the one who called is included in the response.
Barchu is said only in the morning service
it opens the Shema's blessings morning and evening, and comes before each Torah reading.

games.q: you're leading prayer and you reach Barchu. only eight people are in the room. what happens?
o: skip the call; it needs ten.
count the chairs as two more.
games.why: the Talmud teaches any matter of holiness needs ten. without a minyan, the call isn't said, and each person continues on their own.

practice: Think of the voices that call to you in a day: the ones you answer fast, like an alarm or a boss, and the ones left hanging, like a friend who texted twice or a child asking you to come look.
Pick one, picture the person on the other end, and picture yourself answering the way a room answers Barchu: all at once, and glad to.

wordCard.voice: Barchu. Bless: the leader's call to prayer, answered by the congregation, said only with a minyan of ten.

orig.note: Hebrew: bless! a command, said to many people at once.

carryVoice: Your line: answer the call. It takes ten to say it, and everyone gets to answer. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt His name together.
